doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Early records at home and the effects of music on children
summary: Jimmy recalls his uncle's records in Buffalo and the home piano; talk turns to music's effect on children and simple chords.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And that’s where I became — it struck a chord here. And that’s it, I said I knew what I wanted to do. Which actually it was an affirmation really, and a confirmation. Because at home, before even getting into school, when I was like four and five years old — two and say three, after — I was born in Birmingham, Alabama but I came there when I was about three years old, two and a half to three years. But anyway, my uncle, in Buffalo, New York, had all the records. And the word — I didn’t know it then, but — he was looking back, he was a very eclectic — he had a very eclectic ear. He had from country, spirituals, to opera, Lawrence Tibbett and I always recall her name, but Lily Pons. You know that’s going back you know.
You never thought you’d say that, did you?
No, no. Because I’m watching his eyes. And naturally Caruso you see. And just name it, I heard all these, all this. And then we had the piano at the house—
Everybody had a piano at that time. Everybody had a piano.
Yeah, at that time. It’s like everybody in the south had an organ way back earlier, you know what I mean? Had a little pump organ.
And now they’ve just begun to gather data about what that does to a child’s spatial knowledge by — it has to do with music.
And I’m not going out of here without them knowing that. Because we’ve said it for years, and so we’ve lived it.
And our structures, that’s why you heard me say that — I didn’t know you hadn’t heard that, three dimensions, depth, breadth and height. Because you’re dealing with a pyramid there.

I’m going to pause for one second—This curtain was too close and it’s rubbing the back of your head. You okay? So we’ll just pick up, we’ll edit that out. That’s so true with the education and sometimes I see kids who have a really hard time even clapping or moving to a beat. And I’m going, why is that? I want to know why that is. And I suspect it’s because they don’t have music in the house.

Because it’s like we’re more mass conscious I would say as of now, we’re becoming much more aware of being aware of the power of music. Because what it can do subliminally, without any overt influences, is amazing. We haven’t gotten to that yet.

Well then do you feel that the negative influence is also possible? I mean there’s a kind of controversy about a lot of the music that’s out today, whether it be rap or heavy metal — some of the things that they’re saying — if music can be a positive influence, can it also go the other way?

I don’t really know. All I know is that some of the studies that I’ve been following find that the more simple, the simpler the music is, the more the child learns, even in utero. Like just a plain little chord — a 1-3-5 chord and maybe a 7th you know, later. And the simpler the music is, it seems to widen their spatial sense. And then they also find that vocal music also. But it has to be a certain type, simple again you see. So I have a feeling that they’re going to find that each one of the chords have a power and really correspond to a part of the person’s brain and body. So I’m thinking that pretty soon — they can measure this stuff now, I know they can.
